newsitem.title: USA: U.S. govt to fund search for abducted children.
newsitem.headline: U.S. govt to fund search for abducted children.

text.p: The U.S. government announced on Thursday that it would in future pay for needy American parents to travel abroad to try to recover children abducted by estranged spouses.

The move is one of a range of measures agreed by the State and Justice Departments to expand a programme begun last year to recover American children, about 1,000 of whom are abducted or illegally kept abroad each year by non-custodial parents.
Travel costs will be paid for parents "who can prove that dire economic hardship prevents them from recovering their children from overseas," the State Department said.

The measures aim to combat what department spokesman Nicholas Burns called an "increasingly serious problem" of parents who have been denied custody after a marriage break-up spiriting their children abroad.

"Often such abductions involve international marriages that are dissolving when one parent returns to his or her native country and abducts the child in violation of the other parent's custody rights," the department said.

Aileen Adams, director of the Justice Department's Office for Victims of Crime (OVC), said that "many parents have exhausted their life savings on telephone calls, attorneys and private investigators in the search for their children."
She said the programme would "provide immeasurable help to these parents and their children."

The Justice Department said the travel expenses would be paid for by the OVC. A spokeswoman, Mari Ann Hollis, put the annual budget for this and other services provided under the programme at $450,000.

Child abductions come under an international treaty known as the Hague Convention, signed by 43 countries, which provides for the prompt return of wrongfully removed or retained children to the country of their "habitual residence."
But according to State Department figures, only about 60 percent of the children abducted from the United States are taken to signatory countries.

"In some cases, other countries don't take this problem seriously," Burns told a news briefing. "They harbour the people who have abducted the children. They don't give the parent with whom the child is living any kind of rights within that country."

Noting that there were "a number of countries where this habitually takes place," he promised a concerted effort to persuade them to sign the Hague Convention. The spokesman did not name the countries.

The State and Justice Departments said they were working with a private non-profit group, the National Centre for Missing and Exploited Children, to find missing children and help parents obtain lawful custody.
Other services the departments said they would provide included:
-- legal assistance to explain the Hague Convention;
-- contacts abroad through the international police organisation Interpol and other agencies;
-- volunteer assistance to translate foreign language correspondence and conversations;
-- distribution of posters in target countries to help find missing children.
